query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Local composition gradients at the nanoparticle surfaces lower the local melting temperature, so that early premelting initiates at compositionally inhomogeneous regions, which then propagate into full melting of the FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, well-mixed FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles synthesized via rapid thermal shock to achieve a disordered solid solution.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ heating experiments using TEM or synchrotron X-ray diffraction on size-selected nanoparticles under controlled atmospheric conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in a vacuum or inert environment with carefully regulated heating rates approaching the premelting and melting temperature regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Local surface compositional variations that create heterogeneous surface energies across the nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: Local deviations in elemental distribution at the nanoparticle surface reduce the local melting point, causing selective early-stage surface premelting that then triggers further melting of the nanoparticle core.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles exhibiting local chemical inhomogeneity will show earlier and spatially non-uniform melting at the surface when heated, compared to nanoparticles with a more uniform composition which would melt more uniformly at the baseline melting temperature.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with an initially homogeneous alloy composition are expected to display uniform melting onset near the predicted bulk melting point.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected under high-temperature conditions just below and into the melting regime and may be influenced by the heating rate; the test is valid as long as the nanoparticles remain in an inert or vacuum environment (to prevent surface oxidation) and below temperatures where significant evaporation occurs.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative correlation between local compositional gradients and premelting onset is expected, the magnitude of the effect and the precise temperature shifts may vary with nanoparticle size, heating rate, and exact compositional deviations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one with intentionally enhanced local compositional segregation (e.g., induced by controlled partial annealing or chemical treatments) and one with as-synthesized homogeneous alloying. Heat both sets in situ under identical controlled conditions while recording high-resolution TEM images and compositional maps (via EDS) in real time.
measurements: Spatially resolved TEM imaging of the nanoparticle surfaces to detect the onset and progression of melting.
EDS or similar elemental mapping to correlate regions of compositional inhomogeneity with early melting features.
Temperature measurements to document the exact temperature at which premelting features appear.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets of nanoparticles show a uniform onset of melting that is independent of initial compositional heterogeneity (i.e., no correlation between local composition gradients and premelting onset), then the hypothesis that local composition gradients govern the early stage of melting will be falsified.

In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c. Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).

AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. decision.trend: Recent studies on high-entropy alloy nanoparticles exposed to high-temperature processing (particularly works reporting direct observation of multi-element metallic nanoparticle formation and stabilization under rapid heating or laser-based processes) highlight two main efforts: (1) in situ, high-temperature exposures that reveal partial melting and re-solidification steps, and (2) advanced, rapid synthesis techniques (e.g., laser solid-phase routes) that create nanoparticles but leave open questions about the early onset of local melting phenomena. While these approaches have successfully visualized nanoparticle evolution and provided valuable insights into diffusion pathways, local phase segregation, and morphological changes, they have not conclusively resolved how complex elemental interactions in FeNiCrCoCu drive the precise temperature at which premelting starts. Key gaps remain in connecting local composition fluctuations, interface structure, and atomic transport to the observed variations in premelting temperature and progression.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how local elemental segregations, surface energy variations, and interface structures jointly govern the initial formation of liquid-like regions and subsequent melting progression in solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under elevated temperatures, complicating prediction of their usable temperature range and controlling synthesis conditions.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ heating TEM or synchrotron X-ray diffraction experiments on size-selected FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, measuring real-time structural evolution and compositional redistribution across the melting transition in controlled vacuum or inert atmosphere at varied heating rates.
decision.why: Direct, spatially resolved observation of the nanoparticles’ morphological and compositional changes under carefully calibrated heating protocols will enable testing the mechanistic hypothesis that the onset of premelting and its propagation are governed by local composition gradients and resulting early surface melting. If the hypothesis is correct, early-stage melting will correlate with local chemical inhomogeneity observed by in-situ imaging and diffraction. A falsifying result would be uniform onset of melting at all interfaces regardless of local composition distribution, indicating that other effects (e.g., global thermodynamics or uniform surface energies) drive the transition.
